In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ ﴿The revelation of the Book, there is no doubt in it, from the Lord of the worlds﴾ ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Rather, it is the truth from your Lord, that you may warn a people to whom no warner had come before you, that they may be guided﴾ ﴿God is the One who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, then He established Himself above the Throne. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from the Lord of the worlds﴾ is connected to "tanzil", so there is an inversion (taqdim and ta'khir) in the speech. It is permissible that it be connected to His saying "la raiba" (no doubt), meaning: there is no doubt in it from the side of God, exalted is He, and even if doubt occurs to the disbelievers, that is not taken into account. Ar-raib means doubt, and it is so throughout the Qur'an except His saying: ﴿the calamities of time﴾ [At-Tur: 30].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do they say﴾ is a transition (idrab), and its estimation is that He said: "Rather, do they say...?" "Iftara'hu" means he fabricated it. Then God, exalted is He, refuted their statement and informed that it is the truth from God, exalted is He. The lam in His saying "li-tundhira" (that you may warn) may be connected to a hidden verb whose estimation is: He sent it down that you may warn, and then one stops at His saying "from your Lord." His saying, exalted is He, ﴿to whom no warner had come﴾ means: no one had directly encountered them, nor had they seen him, nor had their Arab forefathers. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there is no nation but that a warner has passed among them﴾ [Fatir: 24] includes both those who were directly encountered by warners and those who heard of them. Thus the Arabs are among the nations in which warners had passed on this understanding, because they knew of Abraham and his sons, peace be upon them, and their call; yet they had not been reached by a direct warner other than Muhammad ﷺ. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, and Muqatil said: the meaning is: no warner had come to them in the interval (fatra) between 'Isa and Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon them both.

The sound hadiths are consistent in that "creation began on Sunday, and Adam was created on Friday, the last of things." This is consistent with this verse. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (*al-Muharrar al-Wajiz*) on surah 32, verse 5:

God the Exalted said:

﴿He governs the affair from the heaven to the earth; then it ascends to Him in a Day, the measure of which is a thousand years of what you count.﴾

﴿"Al-amr" (the affair)﴾ is a collective noun (*ism jins*) for all affairs. The meaning is: God the Exalted executes His decree concerning all that He wills, and then the report of that returns to Him in a day of the days of this world, whose measure, if a human traveled through it at the ordinary pace of humans, is a thousand years, because the distance between the heaven and the earth is five hundred years. This is one of the opinions, and it is the view of Mujahid, Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Ikrima, and al-Dahhak.

Mujahid also said: the meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿"miqdaruhu" (its measure)﴾ refers to the *tadbir* (governing), that is, the measure of the governing that is completed on the Day of Resurrection is as if a thousand years if a human governed it.

Mujahid also said: the meaning is that God the Exalted governs and conveys to the angels the affairs of a thousand years by our reckoning, and that is one day in His sight. When it is finished, He conveys to them the like of it. So the meaning is that affairs are executed in His sight for this period, and then they finally return to Him, because the final outcome of affairs is with Him.

It was also said: the meaning is that He governs the affair from the heaven to the earth during the period of this world, and then it returns to Him on the Day of Resurrection. The Day of Resurrection has a measure of a thousand years by our reckoning, but for the disbelievers it is the measure of fifty thousand years, because of its terror and horror, as in the surah ﴿"Sa'ala sa'il" (A questioner asked)﴾ [Al-Ma'arij: 1]. There, God willing, we will mention what it contains of interpretations and opinions.

Al-Tabari reported regarding this verse, from some of them, that he said: "His words ﴿in a day﴾ up to the end of the verse (p. 68) are connected to His words before this: ﴿in six days﴾ [As-Sajdah: 4], and are joined to it, meaning that each of those six was a thousand years."

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is a weak opinion, and the wording of this verse is strained by it, and it is rejected by the hadiths that establish the days of God's creation of the creatures. It is also reported from Ibn Zayd, from some of the people of knowledge, that the pronoun in "miqdaruhu" refers to "al-'uruj" (the ascent). Al-'uruj means the ascent, and al-ma'arij are the ladders by which one ascends.

A group said: the meaning of the verse is: He governs the matter of the sun in that it rises and sets in a day, and that is the measure of a thousand years.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This too is weak. The apparent reference of the pronoun in "ilayhi" (to Him) is to the name of God the Exalted, as He said: ﴿I am going to my Lord﴾ [As-Saffat: 99], and as He said: ﴿I am migrating to my Lord﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 26]. All of this is free from any notion of location. It was also said that the pronoun refers to "al-sama'" (the heaven), since it may be mentioned in the feminine.

The majority of readers recited ﴿"ta'uddun" (you count)﴾ with the *ta'* (second person). Al-A'mash and al-Hasan, in one of the reports from him, recited "ya'uddun" with the *ya'* from below (third person).

﴿That is the Knower of the unseen and the seen, the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ ﴿who perfected everything He created, and began the creation of man from clay﴾ ﴿then made his offspring from an extract of base fluid﴾ ﴿then formed him and breathed into him of His spirit, and made for you hearing, sight and hearts; little thanks do you give﴾ ﴿And they say: "When we have gone astray in the earth, shall we indeed be in a new creation?" Nay, they are disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord﴾ ﴿Say: "The angel of death, who has been entrusted with you, will take you back, and then to your Lord you will be returned."﴾

[p-69] A group said: By "the unseen" (al-ghayb) He meant the Hereafter, and by "the seen" (al-shahāda) He meant this world. It was also said: By "the unseen" He meant what is hidden from created beings, and by "the seen" what is witnessed of things. It is as if, by these terms, He encompassed all things.

Most of the people recited "khalaqahu" with a fatḥa on the lām, as a past verb (fiʿl māḍī). The meaning of "aḥsana" is that He perfected and made firm (atqana wa-aḥkama). Thus a thing is "good" in respect of what it is for the purposes for which it is intended. From this meaning is what Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿIkrima said: "The buttocks of the monkey are not beautiful, but they are perfected and firm." The clause "khalaqahu" may be in a position of naṣb (accusative case) as a ṣifa (attribute) of "kull" (every), or in a position of jarr (genitive case) as an attribute of "shay'" (thing). Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr and Ibn ʿĀmir recited "khalqahu" with a sukūn on the lām, and that is in the naṣb as a maṣdar (verbal noun). Its pronoun may refer either to God, the Exalted, or to the object. It is also permissible that it be a badal (substitution, apposition) for "kull". Some people, on this recitation, held that "aḥsana" means "to inspire" (alhama), and that this verse has the same meaning as His saying: ﴿Who gave everything its creation, then guided it﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 50], meaning He inspired the man toward the woman and the camel toward the she-camel. This is a view that is far-fetched, though al-Ṭabarī preferred it.

Most of the people recited "wa-bada'a" (and began). Al-Zuhrī recited "wa-bada khalqa al-insān" with an alif without hamza, and with a naṣb on the qāf. Abū al-Fatḥ said: "That is in the form of a badal, not a taxfīf (lightening by dropping the hamza)."

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

It is as if he substituted the alif for the hamza, and "bidiya" is the dialect of the Anṣār. Ibn Rawāḥa said:

"In the name of God, and by Him we began; even if we worshipped other than Him, we would be wretched."

"Al-insān" (man) is Ādam. He enumerated his affair to his descendants, since his creation is a creation for them, insofar as he is the one who begets them. "Al-nasl" is what comes from an animal as offspring; it seems to be derived from "nasala al-shay'" when it came out of its place. From it is His, may He be blessed and exalted, saying: ﴿and they, from every mound, will hasten forth﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 96]. From it also is "nasala rīsh al-ṭā'ir" when the feathers of the bird fell out. "Al-sulāla" is from "sall yasill": it is as if the water flows out from the man. From this is the saying of the poet:

"She brought him forth, a lion-skinned, lion-hearted one, the offspring of a womb that was not secure."

"Al-mahīn" is the weak; it is said "mahuna al-insān" when a man became weak and humbled.

His saying, may He be exalted, "nafakha" (He breathed) is an expression for pouring the spirit into the body of the son of Ādam. The pronoun in "rūḥihi" (His spirit) refers to God, the Exalted, and it is an idāfa (construct) of ownership to the owner, and of creation to the Creator. Then He made manifest the enumeration of blessings upon them, in that He singled them out in His saying "lakum" (for you), with the pronoun referring to hearing, sight and hearts; and these are also for those previously mentioned. Just as He singled out Ādam with the shaping and the breathing of the spirit, though it is for all of his descendants. All of this is brevity (ījāz), abbreviation (iqtiḍāb), and omission of what is indicated by what is explicitly stated. It is possible that "al-insān" in this verse is a generic noun (ism jins).

His saying, may He be exalted, "qalīlan" is an attribute of an omitted maṣdar, and it is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) when the qualified noun was omitted.

The pronoun in "qālū" refers to the disbelievers who deny the resurrection from the graves, and who consider it remote without proof or evidence. The position of "a-idhā" is naṣb by what is in His saying: ﴿shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾, because its meaning is: "Shall we be restored?" The readers differed concerning "a-idhā", and its full mention has been made before in other than this place.

Most of the readers recited "ḍalalnā" with a fatḥa on the lām. Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū Rajā', Ṭalḥa and Ibn Wathhāb recited "ḍalilnā" with a kasra on the lām. The meaning is: we were destroyed, our joints were severed, and we went away until we were not found. From it is the saying of al-Akhṭal:

His words, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿If only you could see when the criminals bow their heads before their Lord, saying: "Our Lord, we have now seen and heard, so send us back that we may do righteous deeds; indeed we are now certain."﴾ ﴿Had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance, but the word from Me has come into effect: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men all together."﴾ ﴿So taste [the punishment] because you forgot the meeting of this your Day. His words, may He be exalted: "If only you could see" is an expression of wonder directed at Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community regarding the state of the disbelievers and what befell them. The response (jawab) of "law" (lau, "if only") is omitted, because omitting it is more terrifying, as the person is left with his imagination reaching its furthest extent. **Commentary of Ibn ʿAtiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 32, verses 21–22:**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And We will surely make them taste the lesser punishment, short of the greater punishment, so that perhaps they will return.﴾ ﴿And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the signs of his Lord, then turns away from them? Indeed, We will take retribution upon the criminals.﴾

The pronoun in His saying, "We will surely make them taste" (*linudhīqannahum*), refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh. God informed that He would afflict them with a punishment short of the punishment of the Hereafter, so that perhaps they would repent and take heed. There is no disagreement that the greater punishment is the punishment of the Hereafter. The interpreters (*al-mutaʾawwilūn*) differed about identifying the lesser punishment. Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi and Muqatil said: it is the years of famine in which God made them hungry. Ibn ʿAbbas and Ubayy ibn Kaʿb said: it is the calamities of this world, such as illnesses and the like. Ibn Zayd also said this. Ibn Masʿud and al-Hasan ibn ʿAli said: it is killing by the sword, as at Badr and other battles.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

According to this interpretation, the "one who returns" (*al-rājiʿ*) is other than "the one who tastes" (*alladhī yadhūq*), rather it is the one who remains after him, and the ranks of the pronoun of tasting and the pronoun of *laʿalla* differ.

Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, may God be pleased with him, also said: it is the assault (*al-baṭshah*), the lasting punishment (*al-lizām*), and the smoke (*al-dukhān*). Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, also said: by this He meant the prescribed punishments (*al-ḥudūd*).

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

According to this interpretation, it is likely that it applies to the sinful among the believers.

Mujahid said: by this He meant the punishment of the grave.

Then He said, may He be exalted, in the manner of wonder and affirmation: ﴿And who is more unjust?﴾, meaning: no one is more unjust than one who has this description. This is the opposite of what was mentioned earlier concerning the description of the believers, that when they are reminded of the signs of God, they fall down in prostration. Then He threatens the criminals, who are those who boldly commit disbelief and sins by force. The apparent meaning of "criminality" (*ijrām*) here is disbelief.

Al-Tabari related from Yazid ibn Rafiʿ that he said: God's saying in the Qur'an, ﴿Indeed, We will take retribution upon the criminals﴾, refers only to the people of *al-qadar* (predestination).

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

He means those who say that the actions of the servant are created by the servant himself. He said: Then Yazid ibn Rafiʿ recited: ﴿Indeed, the criminals are in error and madness﴾ [al-Qamar: 47] ﴿The day they are dragged into the Fire upon their faces, [it will be said:] "Taste the touch of Saqar"﴾ [al-Qamar: 48] ﴿Indeed, We have created everything by measure﴾ [al-Qamar: 49].

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

In this line of argument there is a distance (from the correct meaning) that is not hidden. Muʿadh ibn Jabal related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Three people who do these have committed a crime: whoever ties a banner for something other than the right, whoever disobeys his parents, or whoever walks with a wrongdoer in support of him."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a weak view.

"Al-miryah" means doubt. The pronoun in "ja'alnāhu" refers to Moses, and this is the view of Qatada; it is also possible that it refers to "the Book."

"A'immah" is the plural of imam, which is one who is followed, and its root is the cord used in building (khayṭ al-bināʾ). The majority of readers read "lammā ṣabarū" with a fatḥa on the lām and a shadda on the mīm, while Ḥamza and al-Kisā'ī read "limā ṣabarū" with a kasra on the lām and lightening of the mīm, and this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, Talha, and al-A'mash. Will they not then see?﴾ ﴿And they say, "When is this victory, if you are truthful?"﴾ ﴿Say, "On the Day of Victory, their faith will not benefit those who disbelieved, nor will they be reprieved."﴾ ﴿So turn away from them and wait; indeed they are waiting.﴾

"Yahdi" means: it makes clear (yubayyin), as said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him. The majority of readers recited "yahdi" with a yā', so the subject is God Most High according to one group, the Messenger according to another group, and the verbal noun (al-masdar) according to another group, as if it said: "Has the guidance not been made clear to them?" The Kufans permitted that the subject be "kam" (how many), but this is not permitted according to the Basrans, because in a declarative statement it has the same rule as in an interrogative, in that what precedes it does not govern it. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman recited "nahdi lahum" with a nūn, which is the reading of al-Hasan and Qatada. Then the subject is God Most High, and "kam" is in the accusative position: according to the Kufans it is governed by "nahdi", and according to the Basrans by "ahlakna", on both readings. The majority of readers recited "yamshūna" with a fatha on the yā' and a light shīn; Ibn al-Sumayfa' al-Yamani recited "yumashshūna" with a ḍamma on the yā', a fatha on the mīm and a doubled shīn; 'Isa ibn 'Umar recited "yumshūna" with a ḍamma on the yā', a sukūn on the mīm and a ḍammed light shīn. The pronoun in "yamshūna" may refer to the addressees of the clear proof who are being argued against, or it may refer to those who were destroyed, so "yamshūna" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: they were destroyed while walking in their dwellings. The pronoun in "yasma'ūna" refers to those who are being warned. The meaning of the verse is establishing the proof against the disbelievers through the earlier nations who disbelieved and were destroyed.

Then the Mighty and Majestic established the proof against them concerning faith in power and in resurrection, by alerting them to the revival of the dead land by water. "Al-sawq" is by means of clouds. "Al-juruz" is the thirsty land which has consumed its vegetation because of thirst and summer heat; from it the word is used for one who eats greedily, a poet said:

؎ A cunning, greedy one, who weeps when he is hungry.

(p-83) As for one who explains it as land that does not produce vegetation, his explanation is not precise. God, exalted be He, encompassed every land that has this characteristic, because the sign and the lesson in it are clear. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and others also said: "al-ard al-juruz" is the land of Abyan, which is in Yemen, and it is land that is watered by torrents, not by rain. The majority of people read "al-juruz" with a ḍamma on the rā'; al-Zajjaj said: it is also read "al-juruz" with a sukūn on the rā'.

Then God, exalted be He, singled out the crops for mention, as an honouring of them, and because they are the greatest of what is sought from vegetation; otherwise, it is known that the eating of livestock is from other than crops, but He placed the crops in the position of vegetation in general, then detailed that with the eating of livestock and the children of Adam. Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash and Abu Haywa recited "ya'kulu" with a yā' below; Ibn Mas'ud recited "tubṣirūna" with a tā' above; the majority of readers recited "yubṣirūna" with a yā'.

Then it is related of the disbelievers that they seek a victory and hasten the decisive judgment between them and the Messenger ﷺ, in a sense of mockery and denial. "Al-fath" means judgment; this is the saying of a group of exegetes, and this is the strongest of the opinions. A group said the reference is to the conquest of Makkah.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak, as it is refuted by the report that disbelievers will not benefit from faith. Thus there remains only that "al-fath" means either the judgment of the Hereafter, which is the saying of Mujahid, or a "decision" in this world, like Badr and the like. God's saying ﴿Say, "On the Day of Victory"﴾ refers to the first victory according to its possible meanings. So the alif and lam in the second "al-fath" are for prior reference, "yawma" is an adverbial of time, its governing element is "yanfa'u", and "yunzarūna" means: they will be delayed.

Then the Blessed and Exalted commanded him to turn away from the disbelievers and to await relief, and this is among what the verse of the sword abrogated. God's saying ﴿Indeed they are waiting﴾ means the punishment, in the sense that this is their ruling, even if they are not aware. Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' recited "muntaẓarūna", meaning: awaited for the punishment descending upon them. And God knows best.

The commentary on Surat al-Sajda is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

And blessings and peace be upon our master Muhammad, and upon his family and all his companions.
